intro: The site is about the cricketer. This page is about the rest: the family, the ticket collector's job, the bikes, the army rank, the retirement message and what the ICC said in June 2025. Everything here is on the public record; nothing is speculated.

sections.title: Ranchi and family
text: He is the youngest child of Pan Singh, who moved from the hills of Uttarakhand (the family is from Lwali village, Almora district) to work at MECON in Ranchi, and Devaki Devi. His brother Narendra is involved in local politics; his sister Jayanti is a teacher.

He married Sakshi Singh Rawat, whose father had worked with his at MECON, on 4 July 2010 in Dehradun, a day after their engagement was announced. Their daughter Ziva was born on 6 February 2015 in Ranchi while he was at the World Cup in Australia; he did not come home until the tournament ended.
He has never moved his base from Ranchi. His farmhouse at Ring Road, Sembo, has a cricket pitch, a motorcycle garage and a farm from which he sells vegetables and strawberries.

sections.title: The Travelling Ticket Examiner
text: From 2001 to 2003 he was a TTE at Kharagpur station in West Bengal, employed by South Eastern Railway under the sports quota, playing for the Railways in domestic tournaments. Colleagues have described him as a quiet, honest ticket checker who played cricket on the station ground.
He left when the Jharkhand selectors and the BCCI's talent wing began to take notice; he has said he would have stayed if cricket had not worked out.

sections.title: The goalkeeper
text: He was a goalkeeper at DAV Jawahar Vidya Mandir and played for district and club sides before the school's cricket coach, Keshav Banerjee, asked him to try keeping wicket. He has said the reflexes and the diving came from goalkeeping. He co-owns Chennaiyin FC in the Indian Super League (since 2014) and Ranchi Rays in hockey.

sections.title: Bikes and cars
text: He owns a large collection of motorcycles, kept at the Ranchi farmhouse, including vintage Yamaha RD350s, a Kawasaki Ninja H2, a Confederate Hellcat and a Harley-Davidson Fat Boy, as well as a Hummer H2, a Pontiac Firebird Trans Am, a Nissan Jonga and a Land Rover 3. He co-owned the Mahi Racing Team in Supersport World Championship (2013). The bikes appear in nearly every interview he has given at home.

sections.title: The Territorial Army
text: In November 2011 he was conferred the honorary rank of Lieutenant Colonel in the Parachute Regiment of the Territorial Army, alongside shooter Abhinav Bindra. In 2015 he completed five parachute jumps from an Indian Air Force aircraft at Agra to earn his para wings. In August 2019, after the World Cup, he spent two weeks with the 106 Para Territorial Army battalion in Kashmir, on patrol and guard duties.

The rank is honorary. He has not served in combat and has never claimed to. He received the Padma Bhushan in 2018 in uniform, and the 'Balidaan' dagger insignia on his wicketkeeping gloves at the 2019 World Cup was removed at the ICC's request because it is a regimental emblem.
sections.source: Indian Army; Press Information Bureau; ICC statement, June 2019

text: On 15 August 2020, Independence Day, at 7.29 pm, he posted a montage of his career on Instagram set to 'Main pal do pal ka shayar hoon' from Kabhi Kabhie, with the caption: 'Thanks a lot for ur love and support throughout. from 1929 hrs consider me as retired'. He was in Dubai at the CSK hotel. Suresh Raina retired minutes later.

He has never explained the time. Theories range from the 2011 final to his jersey number; none has been confirmed. The BCCI statement that evening called it the end of an era. He had not played for India since the Old Trafford semi-final 13 months earlier.
sections.source: @mahi7781 on Instagram, 15 August 2020; BCCI media release

sections.title: ICC Hall of Fame, 2025
text: On 9 June 2025 the ICC inducted him into its Hall of Fame with Hashim Amla, Matthew Hayden, Graeme Smith, Daniel Vettori, Sarah Taylor and Sana Mir, the largest single intake in its history, ahead of the World Test Championship final at Lord's. The citation lists 538 matches and 17,266 runs and records that he is the only captain to have won all three ICC white-ball trophies.

quote.text: It is an honour to be named in the ICC Hall of Fame, which recognises the contributions of cricketers across generations and from all over the world. To have your name remembered alongside such all-time greats is a wonderful feeling.
quote.source: MS Dhoni, ICC media release, 9 June 2025

sections.title: Myths, checked
text: He did not fail an audition as a ticket collector; the job was through the sports quota. He did not play U-19 cricket for India, which is true, and is part of why the 2016 film made so much of the late start. He did not say 'you play for 75 million people', which is a line from the film's screenplay. The 1929 retirement time has no confirmed meaning. The 2011 six was hit at around 10.49 pm IST, not at 19:29.

legacy.title: The wicketkeeper-batter became a job description
legacy.text: Before him Indian selectors picked the best gloveman and hoped he could bat. After 183* and ten ODI hundreds, every Test side in the world wanted a keeper who could win a match; Pant, Buttler, de Kock and Klaasen are the inheritance.

legacy.title: The finisher became a role
legacy.text: Franchise teams now recruit for the No.6 who bats to the last over. The 84 not-outs and the preference for taking the chase to the final over are the model, for better and worse.

legacy.title: Calm became a captaincy style
legacy.text: Kohli's aggression was framed against it; Rohit Sharma's quiet, long-game captaincy at Mumbai and for India is closer to the Dhoni original. Both have said they learned the job from him.

legacy.title: A franchise became a culture
legacy.text: CSK's retention-first, experience-over-youth method is a direct product of his view of T20, and the yellow in away grounds is the clearest sign that a club identity can exist in Indian cricket.

legacy.title: Ranchi became a cricket city
legacy.text: The JSCA International Stadium opened in 2013 with a stand named for him; Jharkhand had produced no Test cricketer before him. Ishan Kishan and Saurabh Tiwary followed.

closing.text: You came for the runs and the dismissals and stayed for the spirit. You leave knowing why calm can conquer chaos, and why one man from Ranchi changed what an Indian cricketer could be.
